label: Support Functions
notes: Open by presenting the support function as a fingerprint of a set. Instead of listing all points of C, we ask every direction u how far C reaches under the linear probe x dot u. The lecture goal is to make that probing idea do real work: support lines, exposed faces, reconstruction, operations, and computation.

label: Linear Probe
notes: Use the polygon to make the definition tactile. For a fixed u, every point receives a score x dot u, and the support value is the largest score. On a polytope the maximum is found among vertices, which is why the finite sampling check in the slide-local JSON is meaningful for this example.

label: Supporting Line
notes: Translate the number h_C(u) into geometry. The inequality x dot u less than or equal to h_C(u) describes a closed halfspace containing C, and the boundary line is where the best score is achieved. Moving u rotates the halfspace and scans the boundary.

label: Exposed Face
notes: The exposed face is the set of all maximizers, not just a single point. A generic direction on a polygon exposes a vertex, while a normal direction perpendicular to an edge exposes the whole edge. This is the bridge from a function value back to visible boundary structure.

label: Polygon Support Map
notes: Read this as a support map rather than a picture of one direction. Each sector of directions has the same exposed vertex, and the support function is linear within that sector. Corners in the support graph mark changes in the active maximizer.

label: Support Of Sum
notes: The Minkowski sum identity is the cleanest operation rule. A linear probe of A plus B separates into one probe on A and one probe on B, so the two best values add. This is why support functions convert set addition into ordinary function addition.

label: Support Of Convex Hull
notes: For a convex hull of a union, a linear function cannot improve by averaging two candidates unless one of them was already at least as good. The support value is therefore the maximum of the support values of the pieces. This slide prepares the operation ledger.

label: Indicator Conjugate
notes: Connect the section to the previous conjugacy section without turning the lecture into abstraction. The indicator function is zero on C and infinite outside C, so its conjugate keeps exactly the supremum of x dot u over C. This explains the notation and the closed-set reconstruction.

label: Halfspace Reconstruction
notes: State the reconstruction theorem as an intersection procedure. For a closed convex set, every support value gives one containing halfspace, and the intersection of all those halfspaces returns the set. If the set is not closed, the same data reconstructs its closure.

label: Boundedness And Finiteness
notes: Separate three ideas that students often blur: finite support values, the barrier cone, and boundedness. The effective domain of h_C is the set of directions with finite upper bound. A nonempty convex set is bounded exactly when every direction has a finite support value.

label: Norm Balls
notes: Use norm balls as familiar support functions. The Euclidean ball gives the Euclidean norm by Cauchy Schwarz, the l1 ball gives the infinity norm, and the infinity ball gives the l1 norm. This is the first concrete hint of polar and gauge geometry in the next section.

label: Numerical Probe Lab
notes: Invite students to treat the support function as executable. Pick a direction, compute all dot products against the vertices, take the maximum, and record which vertex or face is exposed. The residual column is deliberately boring; zero residual means the definition and the finite model agree.

label: Operation Ledger
notes: This slide is the compact toolkit. Each row says what a set operation becomes after taking support functions and what hypothesis is being used. The key habit is to ask whether the rule is about sums, maxima, positive homogeneity, or intersection of halfspaces.

label: Recap
notes: Close by returning to the fingerprint metaphor. A support function records every linear shadow of a closed convex set, exposes its faces, reconstructs it from halfspaces, and makes several set operations algebraic. The next natural move is to compare this with polar sets and gauges.
